transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Hi, thank you. Um, well, I guess I’m here because things have just gotten really... out of hand lately. I teach elementary school, and the days are just so incredibly long and draining, but it's what happens when I get home that's the real problem. I keep having these nights where I eat an amount of food that genuinely scares me. 

It’s like a switch flips or something. I’ll sit down at my kitchen table to grade papers—usually spelling tests or math worksheets, which always takes forever—and I’ll start with just my normal dinner leftovers. I tell myself I'm just having a normal meal while I work. But then it just... it spirals completely out of my control. I end up going back to the kitchen and going through just box after box of cereal, entire sleeves of crackers, just eating peanut butter straight out of the jar with a spoon. I even end up tearing into whatever snacks I packed for my classroom, you know, the little granola bars or fruit snacks I keep in my tote bag for the kids who forget their lunch. It’s just this massive, terrifying amount of food, and I just keep going and going, and it's happening so often now that I just didn't know what else to do but come here.
When you're eating all of that food, do you feel like you're in control of how much you're eating, or does it feel like you can't stop or control yourself once you start?

No, I... I have absolutely no control. None at all. It’s actually the most bizarre, terrifying feeling because, you know, I have a master's degree, I teach children all day about self-regulation and making good choices. We literally have a whole unit on it in my classroom. But when this happens... once I start eating, it's like... it feels like the reasonable, rational teacher part of me is just detached, like I'm watching myself from the outside. 

And that part of my brain is standing there saying, "Joan, stop. What are you doing? Just put the box down." But I can't. My hands just... they act like they have a mind of their own. They just keep opening things, ripping wrappers, untwisting jars, and just putting food in my mouth, over and over. I can hear myself telling me to stop, but I just keep going and going until I’m so painfully full that it actually hurts to sit upright in my chair. Like, my stomach gets so stretched and tight, but even then, my hands are still reaching for more. It's this complete disconnect between my mind and my body, and I just can't make it stop once that switch is flipped. I just sit there and watch myself do it until I physically can't fit another bite.
After these episodes of overeating, do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or exercise excessively to try to make up for the food you ate?

I don't... no, I don't make myself throw up, and I've never taken laxatives or anything like that. The thought of doing that actually really scares me. But... but I do try to fix it. I feel like I absolutely *have* to fix it, because the guilt the next morning is just so heavy, it's literally suffocating. 

So, after one of those nights, I’ll wake up and I’ll make this strict rule for myself. I’ll tell myself I’m absolutely not allowed to eat breakfast. And then I’ll deliberately leave my lunch at home when I go to school. I’ll just sit in the teachers' lounge during my prep period, or while the kids are at lunch, and all the other teachers are eating their salads or heating up their meals, and I just drink black coffee and pretend I'm not hungry. I'll tell them I had a massive breakfast, which is a lie, obviously, but I just feel like I don't deserve food after what I did the night before. I have to punish myself, I guess.

And then... then the exercise part, yeah. As soon as the final bell rings and the buses are gone, I don't even stay in my classroom to grade things. I just have to move. I have this nature trail near my apartment, this really long, steep path, and I'll just go out there and I'll stay out on the trail for hours. I'll just walk and run and push myself up these hills until my legs feel like lead. Or, if it's getting dark, I'll go home and unroll my mat and do extra yoga—like, these really intense, fast-paced power yoga routines, just back to back to back. 

And the crazy part is, I'll be so incredibly shaky from not eating all day, you know? Like my hands are actually trembling, my vision gets kind of spotty, and I'm so exhausted I can barely hold my own body weight up in a pose, but my brain just screams at me that I haven't done enough yet. I just keep pushing and pushing myself through the exhaustion, even when I feel like I might actually pass out, because I feel like I have to burn off every single calorie or I'm just a total failure.
Can you describe what it feels like during these episodes—specifically, does it feel like you're not in control of your actions, like you can't stop eating even though you want to?

Yeah, exactly, it's just like I was trying to explain a minute ago. It's exactly that. Um, I know I kind of went on about it already, but it really is this total, absolute disconnect, and I just can't emphasize enough how terrifying that feeling is. 

Once I start eating, it just completely takes over. Like I mentioned, it feels like the reasonable, adult, teacher part of me is literally just watching the whole thing happen from the outside. I'll be sitting there at my kitchen table, surrounded by all these half-graded math worksheets, and the rational part of my brain is just screaming, "Joan, stop! Just put it down! What are you doing?" But my body just completely ignores me. It's like my hands are completely disconnected from my brain and running on some kind of horrible autopilot. They just keep opening things, tearing into boxes, scooping things out, and putting food in my mouth, over and over and over again. 

I want to stop so badly, I really do, and I'm totally aware of how out of control it is while it's happening, which almost makes it worse, you know? Being aware of it but not being able to change it. I just... I can't stop. I just keep going and going, ignoring my own internal voice begging me to quit, until I'm so painfully full that it literally hurts my stomach. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, knowing you desperately want to stop and just having to watch yourself completely fail to do it.
During these episodes, do you ever feel detached from yourself or like you're not really there, as if you're watching yourself from outside your own body?

Well, no, not... not exactly like that. I know I said earlier that it feels like I'm watching myself from the outside, but it's not like an out-of-body experience, if that's what you mean. Like, I don't feel like I'm floating near the ceiling or anything weird like that. I'm definitely still in my body, still sitting at my kitchen table, still surrounded by my students' papers. I'm very much there, physically. 

It's more just... it's a disconnect between my rational mind and my actions. Like, the part of me that knows better, the part that teaches second graders about self-control, is wide awake and present, but it's just completely powerless to stop my hands from moving. So when I say I feel like I'm watching myself, I just mean that I'm fully aware of what I'm doing, and I'm internally screaming at myself to stop, but my body just won't listen. I'm definitely still in my own skin, feeling the food, feeling my stomach getting tighter and tighter... I just can't make the connection between my brain saying "stop" and my hands actually stopping. So, no, I don't feel detached in a literal sense. I'm very painfully present for the whole thing.
During these episodes, do you ever feel like you're in a daze or not fully aware of what you're doing while you're eating all that food?

Um, no, not really in a daze. I mean, I know some people describe things like that, like they just blank out and suddenly all the food is gone, but for me... no, it's not like that at all. I'm actually hyper-aware of everything. Like, painfully aware. 

I don't zone out or forget what I'm doing. I remember every single thing I open, every wrapper I tear, every bite I take. I can tell you exactly what order I ate things in. Like last Tuesday, I started with the leftover pasta from the fridge, and I remember exactly how cold it was because I didn't even bother to heat it up, and then I moved straight to a family-size bag of tortilla chips, and I can remember the exact crunch and the salt on my fingers, and then it was the pint of ice cream... 

So, yeah, I'm completely, one hundred percent aware. There's no fog, no daze, no blanking out. My brain is fully switched on the entire time, which, honestly, is the absolute worst part of it. Because I'm sitting there, fully conscious, fully realizing that I'm ruining all the hard work I put in during the day—all the starving, all the fasting, all the walking on that trail—and I'm just watching myself do it anyway. It's like my senses are actually dialed up to ten. I can hear myself chewing, I can feel my stomach stretching, I can feel the sugar rush, but I just... I just keep going. So, no, I'm definitely not in a daze. I wish I was, sometimes. It might make the guilt a little easier to handle if I could just pretend I didn't know what was happening, you know? But I know. I always know exactly what I'm doing.
How often do you experience these episodes of losing control over your eating and consuming large amounts of food?

Well, um, it's... it's been happening a lot lately. I mean, if I really sit down and think about it, for the past few months, there has rarely been a week without at least one night where I just completely lose it and eat far, far more than I ever meant to. Sometimes it's more than once a week, but it's almost never less than that. 

It usually happens in the evenings, after I've been at school all day. I'll get home, and I'll be so exhausted from dealing with the kids and the lesson plans, and I'll just start, and then I can't stop. And then, of course, the next day, the guilt is just so overwhelming. I wake up feeling so heavy and disgusting, and I just think, "I have to fix this." So I try to make up for it by not eating anything at school. I'll just drink black coffee in the teachers' lounge and tell everyone I had a huge breakfast, which is a lie, obviously. Or I'll push myself through a really long, grueling walk on the trail behind my apartment, or force myself to do extra yoga, even when my muscles are screaming at me to stop. 

I just... I have to balance it out, you know? But then I get so hungry from not eating all day or exercising so much, and the whole cycle just starts all over again. It's exhausting. It's like my whole life right now is just this constant pendulum swinging between losing control at night and punishing myself for it the next day. I can't even remember the last time I just had a normal week where I didn't have to think about all of this. It's just constant.
Do these episodes of overeating and the way you feel about them cause you a lot of distress, or do they interfere with your daily life, like your job, relationships, or how you take care of yourself?

Well, um... yeah. Yeah, it causes a lot of distress. I mean, honestly, it feels like it's taking over everything. It’s like my entire life—my evenings, my weekends—they all just revolve around either the eating or, more often, trying to undo what I just did. Like, I’ll spend hours on a Saturday just walking and walking on that trail, or doing yoga until I’m practically shaking, just trying to burn off whatever I ate on Friday night. And because I’m spending so much time doing that, I’m falling behind on everything else. 

Like, my grading. I teach second grade, and you wouldn’t think there’s that much to grade, but there is, and I used to be so on top of it. Now, I’m just... I’m slower. I’ll sit down with a stack of spelling tests, and my mind is just racing, calculating calories, or I’m so exhausted from starving myself all day that I can’t even focus on whether a seven-year-old spelled "because" correctly. 

And my friends... I’ve definitely been less present. They’ll want to go out for dinner or drinks, and I just can't. I make up excuses, like I’m too tired or I have too much work, but really, it’s because I can’t handle being around the food, or I know I need that time to exercise. Or if I do go, I’m just sitting there, completely distracted, obsessing over what everyone else is eating and what I’m not allowing myself to eat. I’m physically there, but I’m not really *there*, you know? 

And work... God, work is just a constant source of anxiety now. I’m just so terrified that someone is going to notice. I’m constantly worried about seeming put-together, like I’m this perfect, energetic teacher who has it all under control. I’ll put on extra makeup to hide how tired my eyes look, and I’ll force myself to smile and be bubbly in the teachers' lounge, all while I’m completely empty inside because I haven't eaten anything but black coffee. It takes so much energy just to pretend that I’m functioning normally, and it’s just exhausting. It’s completely exhausting. So, yeah, it definitely interferes with my life. It feels like it *is* my life right now.
When you're in the middle of one of these eating episodes, do you feel like you've completely lost control, as if you can't stop eating no matter how hard you try?

Oh, absolutely. It's... it's exactly like that. It’s the most bizarre, terrifying feeling because, like I was saying earlier about being so hyper-aware, I know exactly what’s happening, but I have absolutely zero power to stop it. It’s like... okay, you know how I mentioned I teach second grade? I’m so used to being in charge, being the one who sets the rules, who keeps everything organized and calm and under control. I have my lesson plans color-coded, for heaven's sake. I am a very put-together person in every other aspect of my life. 

But then, when I'm in my kitchen and one of these episodes starts... all of that just goes completely out the window. Once I start, it honestly feels like the reasonable, organized teacher part of me is just watching from the outside. It's like she's standing right there in the room, watching me, and saying, "Joan, stop. What are you doing? You don't need to eat this, just walk away." I can hear my own voice in my head pleading with me. But my body just won't listen. It’s like my brain and my body completely disconnect from each other. 

My hands just have a mind of their own. They just keep opening things—tearing open cereal boxes, unscrewing jars, ripping through plastic wrappers—and just putting food in my mouth, over and over and over again. I’ll be telling myself to put the spoon down, just put the fork down, go to the bedroom, close the door, but my hand just dips right back into the container anyway. I can't stop. I literally cannot stop myself, no matter how hard I try or how much I'm begging myself to in my head, until I am just... until I'm so painfully full that I feel like my stomach might actually burst. It’s just this total, complete loss of physical control, even though my mind is wide awake and screaming at me to quit. I just can't stop my hands from moving.
On average, how frequently have these episodes occurred over the past few months? Have they happened at least once a week most weeks?

Yeah, um, like I think I was saying earlier... if I really sit down and look at the calendar for the past few months, there has rarely been a week without at least one night where I just... I eat far, far more than I ever meant to. It's definitely at least once a week. Sometimes it's more, but at the bare minimum, it's once a week. 

And it's so predictable now, which is the sad part. The episode happens, usually when I'm just completely drained, and then the very next morning I wake up and I immediately have to start trying to make up for it. That's when I do the whole routine I told you about—not eating a single thing at school, just hiding behind my coffee mug in the lounge while the other teachers eat their lunches and talk about their days. Or, if it's the weekend, I'll wake up and immediately push myself through a really long, punishing walk on the trail, or I'll unroll my mat and do all that extra yoga until I can barely hold myself up and my arms are shaking. 

It just happens every single week, like clockwork. I’ll think, "Oh, I’m doing so well this week, I've got this under control," and then Thursday night rolls around, I’m exhausted from the kids and the lesson planning, and boom, it happens again. And then Friday I'm starving myself all day to fix it. So, yes, to answer your question, it's definitely most weeks. Honestly, I can't even remember a week since maybe the beginning of the school year where I didn't have at least one night of eating too much followed by a day of desperately trying to undo it all. It just never really stops.
When you're eating during these episodes, do you feel like you're not in control, like you can't stop eating even though you want to?

Yeah, um, like I was saying just a few minutes ago... it's exactly that. It really is this total, terrifying disconnect. I know we just touched on this, but honestly, it’s the hardest part to explain because it just doesn't make any logical sense to me. 

Like I mentioned before, once I start, it truly feels like the reasonable, adult, teacher part of me is just... floating outside of my body. It's like she’s just standing there in the kitchen watching the whole trainwreck happen, yelling, "Joan, stop! What are you doing? Just walk away!" I can hear myself so clearly. 

But it’s like my brain is completely unplugged from my body. I want to stop, I really, really do, but my hands just keep going. They just keep reaching into the pantry, opening things, tearing wrappers, and putting food into my mouth, over and over. It's like I'm on autopilot and someone else programmed the destination. I'll be begging myself to just put the food down and go to my bedroom, but I literally cannot stop eating until my stomach is so stretched and I'm so painfully full that I physically can't take another bite. It’s just... it’s a complete and utter loss of control. I don't even feel like I'm the one driving my own body when it happens. I just have to watch myself do it.
Do you feel a great deal of shame, guilt, or distress about these episodes of eating, even when they’re happening?

Oh, God, yes. The shame is... it's overwhelming. It's honestly the worst part of all of this, even worse than the physical discomfort. It’s just this crushing, suffocating weight that sits right on my chest. Even while it's happening—like I said, when I'm just watching myself tear through the kitchen like a wild animal—I am just so disgusted with myself. I'll be standing there, shoving food in my mouth, and the whole time my inner monologue is just vicious. I'm thinking, "You're pathetic, Joan. Look at you. Look at what you're doing. You're a grown woman, you're a teacher, you have a master's degree, and you can't even stop yourself from eating a whole sleeve of cookies standing over the sink." 

And then afterward... oh, the guilt afterward is just unbearable. I'll look at the empty wrappers on the counter, the dirty plates, the crumbs everywhere, and I just want to crawl out of my own skin. I feel so dirty and so weak. I’ll just sit there on the kitchen floor and cry because I’m so ashamed of what I’ve done. And I have to hide it all, you know? I have to gather up all the wrappers and bury them deep in the trash can under other garbage so if anyone comes over, they won't see the evidence of what a monster I am. 

It bleeds into everything. I feel like an imposter when I go to work the next day. I'm standing up there in front of my second graders, telling them to be good, to make smart choices, to be kind to themselves, and inside I'm just thinking, "If you kids or your parents knew what I did last night... if you knew how out of control and disgusting I am, you wouldn't want me anywhere near this classroom." It’s so isolating. I can't tell anyone about it because the thought of someone else looking at me with the same disgust I feel for myself... I don't think I could survive it. It just eats away at me, this constant, nagging feeling that I'm just fundamentally broken and shameful.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, even outside of these eating episodes?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel hopeless or down in the dumps all the time, you know? Like, outside of the whole food thing, I actually really love my life. I love my job. I mean, teaching second grade is exhausting, don't get me wrong. Some days I come home and I just want to stare at a blank wall for an hour because they have so much energy, but I really do love it. I love seeing their little faces light up when they finally understand a math concept, or when they read a whole sentence by themselves. It's incredibly rewarding. 

And I still really enjoy my hobbies. I mentioned the yoga earlier—even though I sometimes use it to, you know, make up for the eating, I also genuinely just love doing yoga. I have this great studio I go to on Saturday mornings, and the instructor, Sarah, she's just wonderful. She always has this very calming presence, and I love the way I feel after a good class, when it's just for me, not for... punishing myself. I also still love reading. I'm in a book club with a few of the other teachers from school, and we meet up once a month at this little wine bar downtown. We're reading this historical fiction novel right now, and it's so good, I couldn't put it down last weekend. 

So, yeah, I still have things I look forward to. I still laugh with my friends, I still enjoy my weekends, I still care about my students. It's just... it's just this one area of my life that feels like a total disaster zone. The eating and the guilt, that's what brings me down. But if you take that away, if you could just magically erase that part of my brain, I think I'd be a pretty happy, normal person. I don't feel like a depressed person, if that makes sense. I just feel like a person who has this one huge, terrible secret that makes everything else harder. But the rest of my life? The rest of it is actually pretty good.
When you're having one of these eating episodes, do you find yourself eating much more rapidly than normal, or continuing to eat even when you're not really hungry until you feel uncomfortably full?

Um, I’m not really sure, to be completely honest. I’ve never really thought about the speed of it all. I mean, I don't know if I'm eating much more rapidly than a normal person would. When I sit down for a regular meal, like lunch in the breakroom with the other teachers—usually I sit with Sarah from third grade, or Mark who does P.E.—we just eat at a normal pace, you know? It takes maybe twenty or thirty minutes, we talk about our weekends or how the kids are doing, and it's just normal. But when I’m at home in my kitchen during one of these... episodes, I just completely lose track of time. I don't feel like I'm racing against a clock or furiously shoveling it in, I just... I haven't really noticed my hands moving any faster than they normally do. It's more of a steady, unstoppable rhythm than a speed thing, if that makes any sense. I couldn't tell you if it takes ten minutes or an hour because I’m just so zoned out. 

And as for the hunger part... I honestly don't know if I'm physically hungry when it starts. I really couldn't tell you. It's not like my stomach is rumbling or I'm feeling lightheaded from needing a meal. It's like physical hunger doesn't even enter the equation at all. I don't stop and think, "Oh, I'm not hungry, I shouldn't eat." The urge just hits me, and whether my body actually needs food or not is completely irrelevant. I just start eating. 

Like I mentioned before, I definitely keep going until I'm in physical pain from being so full, but how it starts? Whether there was actual hunger there in the first place? I just haven't noticed. It’s all just such a blur. Like last Thursday, I had just gotten home from parent-teacher conferences, which are always so emotionally draining because you have to be "on" for three straight hours, and I walked into the house, dropped my bags, and just went straight to the pantry. I didn't even pause to ask myself if I wanted dinner or if I was hungry. I just don't have that kind of awareness when it happens. I'm just suddenly in it.
Do you usually eat alone during these episodes because you’re embarrassed or ashamed of how much you’re eating?

I mean, I’m not really sure if I can answer that because... well, I don't know if I'm eating alone *because* I'm ashamed, or if it's just because I'm already by myself, you know? 

I live alone in this little one-bedroom apartment over on Elm Street. It’s just me and my cat, Barnaby. I’ve lived there for about two years now, ever since I finished my master's program and got hired at the school. So when I come home at the end of the day, there’s just nobody else around anyway. Usually, after the kids leave at 3:15, I stay in my classroom for another hour or two grading worksheets or prepping for the next day—like, tomorrow we’re starting a unit on the solar system, so I was cutting out all these little foam planets yesterday afternoon—and by the time I finally drive home and unlock my front door, the apartment is just completely empty. 

So, I haven't really noticed if I'm actively seeking out being alone to eat. It's not like I'm out at a restaurant with my friends and I suddenly run off to hide in my car with a bunch of takeout because I don't want them to see me. It just... it happens when I'm already in my kitchen, by myself, in my own space. 

I guess I've never really had to think about it. My mom is always nagging me to get a roommate to save on rent, and sometimes I wonder... I don't know, if I did have a roommate, maybe this wouldn't happen? Or maybe I would just wait until they went to sleep or left for the weekend? I really couldn't tell you. I just haven't had the opportunity to test it out, because I'm just naturally alone when the urge hits. I mean, yes, I am absolutely mortified by what I'm doing, like I said before, but I don't know if that shame is the actual reason I'm alone when I do it. It's just logistics, I guess? I'm alone because I live alone. So I'm really not sure if I'm doing it *in order* to hide, or if the hiding is just a built-in part of my daily routine now.
While you're eating during these episodes, do you feel a sense of relief or pleasure, or does it feel more like something you're compelled to do without any enjoyment?

Pleasure? Oh gosh, no. I mean, maybe for the very first bite? Like, for a split second there's a tiny spark of something, but then it instantly turns into this... this totally mechanical, terrifying thing. You'd think eating all that would be enjoyable, right? Like when I give my second graders a special treat for someone's birthday, they are just over the moon, savoring every single crumb and getting frosting all over their faces. But for me, during these episodes, it’s not about enjoyment at all. It’s exactly like you said, a compulsion. 

It's honestly the strangest, most awful feeling. Once I start, it feels like the reasonable teacher part of me is watching from the outside saying, "Joan, stop," but my hands just keep opening things and putting food in my mouth until I’m painfully full. It's like my body gets completely hijacked. I'm literally hovering there in my own kitchen, looking at myself, and I can't intervene. My hands just have a mind of their own. They're tearing into bags, opening the fridge, grabbing another box, just functioning on this frantic autopilot. I'm not even really tasting the food after a certain point. It's just this unstoppable motion. 

And I just keep going and going until my stomach is physically aching and stretched tight. And the whole time, that logical, organized part of me—the part that color-codes lesson plans and keeps twenty seven-year-olds in line—is just trapped behind glass, watching the disaster happen, and I can't do a single thing to hit the brakes. So, no, there is absolutely no relief or pleasure in it. It's just exhausting and really scary to feel that disconnected from your own actions.

It's not like my stomach is rumbling or I'm feeling lightheaded from needing a meal. It's like physical hunger doesn't even enter the equation at all. I don't stop and think, "Oh, I'm not hungry, I shouldn't eat." The urge just hits me, and whether my body actually needs food or not is completely irrelevant. I just start eating. 

Like I mentioned before, I definitely keep going until I'm in physical pain from being so full, but how it starts? Whether there was actual hunger there in the first place? I just haven't noticed. It’s all just such a blur. Like last Thursday, I had just gotten home from parent-teacher conferences, which are always so emotionally draining because you have to be "on" for three straight hours, and I walked into the house, dropped my bags, and just went straight to the pantry. I didn't even pause to ask myself if I wanted dinner or if I was hungry. I just don't have that kind of awareness when it happens. I'm just suddenly in it.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient eats alone during these episodes due to embarrassment or shame, which would support the diagnosis of binge eating disorder.
doctor.question: Do you usually eat alone during these episodes because you’re embarrassed or ashamed of how much you’re eating?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about eating alone due to embarrassment, which is a symptom of binge eating episodes (typically a specific BED criterion). This specific manifestation is not included in my provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean, I’m not really sure if I can answer that because... well, I don't know if I'm eating alone *because* I'm ashamed, or if it's just because I'm already by myself, you know? 

I live alone in this little one-bedroom apartment over on Elm Street. It’s just me and my cat, Barnaby. I’ve lived there for about two years now, ever since I finished my master's program and got hired at the school. So when I come home at the end of the day, there’s just nobody else around anyway. Usually, after the kids leave at 3:15, I stay in my classroom for another hour or two grading worksheets or prepping for the next day—like, tomorrow we’re starting a unit on the solar system, so I was cutting out all these little foam planets yesterday afternoon—and by the time I finally drive home and unlock my front door, the apartment is just completely empty. 

So, I haven't really noticed if I'm actively seeking out being alone to eat. It's not like I'm out at a restaurant with my friends and I suddenly run off to hide in my car with a bunch of takeout because I don't want them to see me. It just... it happens when I'm already in my kitchen, by myself, in my own space. 

I guess I've never really had to think about it. My mom is always nagging me to get a roommate to save on rent, and sometimes I wonder... I don't know, if I did have a roommate, maybe this wouldn't happen? Or maybe I would just wait until they went to sleep or left for the weekend? I really couldn't tell you. I just haven't had the opportunity to test it out, because I'm just naturally alone when the urge hits. I mean, yes, I am absolutely mortified by what I'm doing, like I said before, but I don't know if that shame is the actual reason I'm alone when I do it. It's just logistics, I guess? I'm alone because I live alone. So I'm really not sure if I'm doing it *in order* to hide, or if the hiding is just a built-in part of my daily routine now.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a sense of relief or pleasure during the eating episodes, which can help differentiate between binge eating disorder and other conditions.
doctor.question: While you're eating during these episodes, do you feel a sense of relief or pleasure, or does it feel more like something you're compelled to do without any enjoyment?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start, it feels like the reasonable teacher part of me is watching from the outside saying, 'Joan, stop,' but my hands just keep opening things and putting food in my mouth until I’m painfully full.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the eating feels like a compulsion (something the patient is compelled to do), which directly relates to the sense of lack of control during the binge eating episode.

patient.answer:
Pleasure? Oh gosh, no. I mean, maybe for the very first bite? Like, for a split second there's a tiny spark of something, but then it instantly turns into this... this totally mechanical, terrifying thing. You'd think eating all that would be enjoyable, right? Like when I give my second graders a special treat for someone's birthday, they are just over the moon, savoring every single crumb and getting frosting all over their faces. But for me, during these episodes, it’s not about enjoyment at all. It’s exactly like you said, a compulsion. 

It's honestly the strangest, most awful feeling. Once I start, it feels like the reasonable teacher part of me is watching from the outside saying, "Joan, stop," but my hands just keep opening things and putting food in my mouth until I’m painfully full. It's like my body gets completely hijacked. I'm literally hovering there in my own kitchen, looking at myself, and I can't intervene. My hands just have a mind of their own. They're tearing into bags, opening the fridge, grabbing another box, just functioning on this frantic autopilot. I'm not even really tasting the food after a certain point. It's just this unstoppable motion. 

And I just keep going and going until my stomach is physically aching and stretched tight. And the whole time, that logical, organized part of me—the part that color-codes lesson plans and keeps twenty seven-year-olds in line—is just trapped behind glass, watching the disaster happen, and I can't do a single thing to hit the brakes. So, no, there is absolutely no relief or pleasure in it. It's just exhausting and really scary to feel that disconnected from your own actions.

The frequency of episodes meets the threshold of at least once per week for several months, fulfilling criteria for binge-eating disorder.
